title: Why Almost Nobody Lives in Most of Nevada

paragraphs.text: Nevada is bigger than Great Britain. About three million people live in it. And almost nine out of ten of them live in just two places: Las Vegas in the far south, and Reno up against the mountains in the west. Everything in between, hundreds of miles of it, is almost empty. At night, from orbit, you can see it. Two lights, and darkness.

shots.photo: File:Las Vegas strip from the air (3191356789).jpg

stat.label: Nevadans living in Clark and Washoe counties, 2020 census (our sum)
stat.source: US Census 2020 (Nevada Legislative Counsel Bureau; Census QuickFacts)

shots.photo: File:Us Route 50 The Loneliest Road In America (225539129).jpeg
shots.on_screen_text: US Route 50, 'the loneliest road in America'

paragraphs.text: The main highway across the middle of the state, US Route 50, has a nickname. In July 1986 LIFE magazine called the stretch from Fernley to Ely the loneliest road in America, quoting a motoring official who could find nothing out there worth stopping for. Nevada did not complain. It printed the phrase on souvenirs and turned it into a slogan.

shots.photo: File:Us Route 50 The Loneliest Road In America (225539129).jpeg
shots.on_screen_text: US Route 50, 'the loneliest road in America'
Eureka and the empty basins around it

paragraphs.text: It is not that nobody ever tried. A lake nearly as big as Lake Erie once filled the northwest of this state, and it vanished. Towns of thousands rose on silver and gold, and blew away within a few years. And today the federal government owns about four fifths of the land, including a stretch of desert it used to set off nuclear bombs. So why does almost nobody live in most of Nevada? There are five reasons. The first one is a wall.

ask.text: Why is most of Nevada empty?

chapters.title: The Wall That Takes the Rain

paragraphs.text: Reason one. The mountains take the rain. Weather in this part of America comes from the Pacific. Wet air rolls in off the ocean and hits a wall: the Sierra Nevada, a range of granite peaks more than fourteen thousand feet high, right along the California border. The air rises, cools, and drops its water on the western slopes. Snow piles up there by the meter. By the time that air comes down the other side, into Nevada, there is very little left.

shots.photo: File:North Lake Tahoe Aerial photo Don Ramey Logan.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Lake Tahoe, on the crest of the Sierra
The west side of Lake Tahoe
East of the Sierra, near Carson City

paragraphs.text: This is called a rain shadow, and Nevada lives in it. The government's climate scientists put it bluntly: Nevada is the nation's driest state. Across the whole state, the average is about ten inches of rain and snow a year. In the southern lowlands it is closer to four. Up on the high peaks of the Sierra it is more than fifty. Same air, a few dozen miles apart.

shots.on_screen_text: The dry side of the Sierra

document.text: Nevada is the Nation's driest state. Statewide annual average (1895–2024) precipitation is only 10.2 inches.
document.source: NOAA NCICS, State Climate Summary: Nevada

chart.title: Yearly rain and snow in Nevada
chart.source: NOAA NCICS, State Climate Summary: Nevada

shots.photo: File:Black Rock Desert 1.300.dpi (24995335682).jpg

paragraphs.text: And it is not one wall. Nevada is made of them. Drive across the state and the road climbs a mountain range, drops into a flat dry valley, climbs another range, drops again, over and over, dozens of times. Geologists call it the Basin and Range. Each range squeezes a little more water out of the sky for itself, and each valley floor gets less. The towns that do exist sit where a stream comes down off a mountain, and almost nowhere else.

shots.photo: File:Us Route 50 The Loneliest Road In America (225539129).jpeg
shots.on_screen_text: US Route 50, 'the loneliest road in America'
The Basin and Range, central Nevada

shots.photo: File:Great Basin National Park - 53837533696.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Ely, at the foot of the Egan Range

paragraphs.text: The high ranges are islands of a different climate, cooler and a little wetter than the desert below. On Wheeler Peak, in what is now Great Basin National Park, grow bristlecone pines, some of the oldest living things on Earth. In August 1964 a graduate student, with the Forest Service's permission, cut one of them down to count its rings. The National Park Service says the tree, later named Prometheus, was about four thousand nine hundred years old. Twenty-two years later the mountain became a national park.

shots.on_screen_text: Wheeler Peak, Great Basin National Park

shots.photo: File:Great Basin National Park - 53837789943.jpg

stat.label: Estimated age of the Prometheus bristlecone pine, cut in 1964
stat.source: National Park Service, The Prometheus Story

shots.on_screen_text: The Snake Range and Great Basin National Park

paragraphs.text: Reason two. What little water there is goes nowhere. Almost all of Nevada lies inside the Great Basin, the largest region in North America where rivers never reach the sea. Rain that falls here stays here. It runs downhill into a valley and stops, and the sun takes it back. Look at the Humboldt River. It rises in the mountains of northeast Nevada and runs west across almost the whole state. And then it simply ends, in a dry flat called the Humboldt Sink.

stat.label: Rivers in the Great Basin that reach the sea

shots.photo: File:Humboldt River Papa 2.jpg

paragraphs.text: It was not always like this. At the end of the last ice age, a lake covered more than eight thousand five hundred square miles of northwestern Nevada, nearly the size of Lake Erie and in places some nine hundred feet deep. Geologists call it Lake Lahontan. You can still see its old shorelines, cut like bathtub rings into the mountainsides. Then the climate dried, and the lake broke into pieces that shrank and disappeared. Only two real lakes are left: Pyramid Lake and Walker Lake.

stat.label: Lake Lahontan at its peak, about 12,700 years ago

shots.on_screen_text: Black Rock Desert, an old lake floor

shots.photo: File:Black Rock Desert 1.300.dpi (24995335682).jpg
File:ISS-32 Walker Lake, Nevada.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Walker Lake from the International Space Station (NASA)

paragraphs.text: Even those two have been fought over. In 1905, in one of the first projects of the new federal Reclamation Service, Derby Dam was built across the Truckee River east of Reno. It sent part of the river into a canal to water farms around Fallon, in the middle of the desert. Less water reached Pyramid Lake, and the lake fell. Its sister, Winnemucca Lake, which had been filled by Pyramid's overflow, dried up completely. In Pyramid Lake lives a fish found nowhere else, the cui-ui, which the Paiute people had fished for generations. It has been on the endangered species list since 1973.

shots.on_screen_text: Derby Dam on the Truckee River
The dry bed of Winnemucca Lake

shots.photo: File:Tufa Rocks, Pyramid Lake, Nevada MET DP242995.jpg

stat.label: Year the cui-ui, found only in Pyramid Lake, was listed endangered
stat.source: US Fish and Wildlife Service, via truckeeriver.org

paragraphs.text: Without rivers that run all year, there is little to farm. Most of Nevada's land is too dry, too salty or too steep to grow a crop without water brought in from somewhere else. The valleys that are green are green because of a single stream, a spring, or a well. Everywhere else is sagebrush, and cattle need a lot of it.

shots.photo: File:Pyramid Lake in Bloom (153466).jpg
File:Rural dirt road in cattle ranch area.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason three. The rush came, and then it left. In 1859, prospectors found silver and gold near what became Virginia City: the Comstock Lode. By 1874, by the National Park Service's count, Virginia City had about twenty-five thousand people, with mansions, an opera house and newspapers. And then the ore ran thin. At the 1880 census the town had fewer than eleven thousand. By 1940 it was down to about five hundred.

shots.photo: File:Virginia City, Nevada - 2025.jpg

stat.label: Virginia City's population by 1874
stat.source: National Park Service, Virginia City Historic District

paragraphs.text: And the whole state went with it. At the 1880 census Nevada had about sixty-two thousand people. Ten years later it had fewer than forty-six thousand, and by 1900 about forty-two thousand. A state shrinking, while the rest of America grew. It would take the next century, and a very different kind of town, to fill it up again.

chart.title: Nevada's population
chart.source: US census, as compiled by Britannica and state histories

shots.photo: File:Tonopah, Nevada LCCN2007662611.tif

paragraphs.text: The story repeated across the desert. Look at Rhyolite, near the California line. In 1904 two prospectors found quartz, in the words of the National Park Service, full of free gold. Within three years Rhyolite had electricity, a mill crushing three hundred tons of ore a day, a school for two hundred and fifty children, and a three-storey bank building that cost ninety thousand dollars. Then came the financial panic of 1907. By 1910 only six hundred and eleven people were left. The mine closed the next year.

paragraphs.text: Tonopah, Goldfield, dozens of camps whose names are now just dots on a map. A mining town lives exactly as long as the ore under it. When it runs out, there is nothing else here to keep people: no farmland, no river, no port. So they leave, and the desert takes the buildings back.

shots.photo: File:Photographs of crowds watching a parade in Tonopah, Nevada circa 1910s.tif
File:Myers Mountain and the eastern skyline of Goldfield in Esmeralda County, Nevada in October 2026.jpg
File:Rhyolite NV Ghost Town - 52133328814.jpg

paragraphs.text: Reason four. Most of Nevada was never handed out. When the West was settled, the federal government gave away or sold land to homesteaders, railroads and states. In Nevada, few people wanted dry sagebrush, and most of it stayed with Washington. Today, by the count of Congress's own research service, about eighty percent of Nevada is federal land, the highest share of any state. Most of it is run by the Bureau of Land Management, as open range for grazing, mining and recreation.

shots.photo: File:Walking Box Ranch, Cattle Loading Gate - panoramio.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A cattle loading gate, southern Nevada

stat.label: Share of Nevada owned by the federal government

shots.photo: File:Rural dirt road in cattle ranch area.jpg

paragraphs.text: That open range has some unusual tenants. By the Bureau of Land Management's own estimate in 2025, about seventy-three thousand wild horses and burros roam public land in the American West, and about thirty-five thousand of them, nearly half, are in Nevada. Out here, wild horses outnumber the people in whole counties.

stat.label: Wild horses and burros on Nevada's public land, nearly half the US total
stat.source: Bureau of Land Management, 2025 population estimates

shots.photo: File:Walking Box Ranch, Cattle Loading Gate - panoramio.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A cattle loading gate, southern Nevada

paragraphs.text: And some of it was set aside for something else entirely. Sixty-five miles north of Las Vegas lies the Nevada Test Site. Between 1951 and 1992, the United States set off nine hundred and twenty-eight nuclear tests here, a hundred in the open air and the rest underground. The US Geological Survey calls Yucca Flat the most cratered landscape on Earth. From orbit it looks like the Moon.

stat.label: Nuclear tests at the Nevada Test Site, 1951-1992

document.text: The most cratered landscape on Earth.

paragraphs.text: Next door is another piece of empty land the government chose for a hard job. In 1987 Congress picked Yucca Mountain, on the edge of the test site, as the only place to study for a permanent dump for the country's spent nuclear fuel. Tunnels were dug. Nevada fought it for two decades. In 2010 the Department of Energy wound the program down, and no high-level waste has ever been stored there. The empty desert was the reason it was chosen, and the people of Nevada were the reason it stopped.

shots.on_screen_text: Yucca Mountain and the test site
The tunnel entrance at Yucca Mountain

shots.photo: File:Myers Mountain and the eastern skyline of Goldfield in Esmeralda County, Nevada in October 2026.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Goldfield, a town on the road past the site

paragraphs.text: The biggest hole is this one. On the sixth of July 1962, a hundred-and-four-kiloton device buried under the desert was set off as a test of using bombs to dig canals and harbors. It left the Sedan crater: twelve hundred and eighty feet across and three hundred and twenty feet deep. Land like this will not be settled. Neither will the ranges and bombing grounds around it. Together, the military holds millions of acres of southern Nevada.

stat.label: Width of the Sedan crater (320 ft deep), 6 July 1962

shots.on_screen_text: The north end of Yucca Flat

paragraphs.text: So who does live in Nevada? Mostly, people who brought their water with them. Las Vegas sits in one of the driest valleys in the country. It exists because of Hoover Dam and Lake Mead, the reservoir behind it on the Colorado River. By the local water authority's own figure, about ninety percent of southern Nevada's water comes from the Colorado. Look at the white ring around Lake Mead. That is how far the water has dropped. Full, the lake stands at about twelve hundred and twenty feet above sea level. In 2022, and again in the summer of 2026, it fell to about one thousand and forty, its lowest since it first filled in 1937, around a quarter full. A city of two million rests on that line. In 1940 the city of Las Vegas had about eight thousand four hundred people. At the 2020 census it had more than six hundred and forty thousand, inside a metro area of over two million.

paragraphs.text: Reno and Carson City do the same in the north, on the Truckee and Carson rivers that run down from the Sierra snow. And in the northeast, around Elko, the desert pays in a different way: gold. Nevada mines most of the gold produced in the United States, from deep pits along a belt called the Carlin Trend. The pits employ thousands, but many workers drive in and out, and the towns stay small.

shots.photo: File:Reno skyline.JPG

shots.on_screen_text: Gold mines on the Carlin Trend

shots.photo: File:Twin Creeks mine Nevada Carlin-type gold ore.jpg

paragraphs.text: And once a year, for about a week, Nevada's emptiness becomes a city. On the dry bed of old Lake Lahontan in the Black Rock Desert, the Burning Man festival builds a temporary town for some seventy thousand people, under a federal permit that allows up to eighty thousand. Then everyone packs up and leaves, and the playa is empty again. It is the clearest picture of the whole state: people can come, but very few can stay.

shots.photo: File:Black Rock Desert 1.300.dpi (24995335682).jpg

stat.label: People at Burning Man in 2024, on a BLM permit for up to 80,000
stat.source: Bureau of Land Management permit; press reports

paragraphs.text: And long before any of them, the Great Basin had people. The Northern Paiute, the Washoe and the Western Shoshone lived across this land for thousands of years, moving with the seasons between the lakes, the piñon pine hills and the valleys. They lived with the desert's limits instead of fighting them. That may be the real lesson of Nevada.

shots.photo: File:Paiute women.jpg
File:Great Basin National Park - 53837789943.jpg

paragraphs.text: So put it together. Mountains that take the rain. Rivers that end in the sand. A lake that dried up. Silver and gold that ran out. And a federal landlord holding four fifths of the state. Nevada is not empty by accident. Its people live where the water is, and the water is almost nowhere.

shots.photo: File:Rhyolite NV Ghost Town - 52133584170.jpg
File:Us Route 50 The Loneliest Road In America (225539129).jpeg
shots.on_screen_text: US Route 50, 'the loneliest road in America'

paragraphs.text: Here is my question for you. If you could live anywhere in Nevada, would you pick the lights of Las Vegas, or a ranch at the end of a hundred-mile dirt road?

shots.photo: File:Las Vegas strip from the air (3191356789).jpg
File:Rural dirt road in cattle ranch area.jpg

ask.text: Las Vegas, or the empty middle?

youtube.title: Why Almost Nobody Lives in Most of Nevada
youtube.description: Nevada is bigger than Great Britain, yet almost nine in ten Nevadans live in just two counties, around Las Vegas and Reno. This video goes through the five reasons the rest stayed empty: the Sierra Nevada rain shadow that makes Nevada the driest state, a Great Basin whose rivers never reach the sea, the silver and gold rushes that came and went, a federal government that still owns about 80 % of the land, including the Nevada Test Site, and the few places where people found water.
